extracted.intended_audience: general readers, film enthusiasts, and researchers seeking information on the film Bridesmaids and its production/reception
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evaluative points that appear in a Wikipedia article about a comedy film; covers production techniques, critical reception, commercial performance, awards, and cultural significance relevant to judging or producing comedic films.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screenplay quality / writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise for Wiig and Mumolo's screenplay appears repeatedly; the screenplay was nominated for Best Original Screenplay and later ranked 12th in the WGA's 101 Greatest Screenplays of the 21st Century.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative remarks emphasize strong, 'brilliantly written' screenplay and its contribution to the film's success. Screenplay recognition (award nominations, WGA rankings) is used as an objective indicator of writing quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performances and acting (lead and supporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular praise for Melissa McCarthy's performance (multiple nominations/wins) and positive notices for Kristen Wiig and the ensemble; McCarthy singled out with Academy, BAFTA, SAG, and critics' awards recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acting is assessed via critics' reviews, awards nominations/wins, and commentary about standout performances. Ensemble strength is noted (e.g., 'Best Acting Ensemble' nominations/wins) as a dimension of quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend of gross-out gags with pathos (humor mix)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rotten Tomatoes consensus: 'A marriage of genuine characters, gross out gags, and pathos' — the combination of physical/gross-out comedy with emotional depth is cited as central to the film's success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective comedies may combine visceral, crude humor with character-based emotion and pathos; this balance is presented as a positive ingredient. Examples: the film's gross-out sequences coupled with character vulnerability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and frequency of raunchy / gross-out humor (polarizing factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some critics praise the film's raunchiness as evidence women can match men in vulgarity; others criticize the frequency and crassness of such jokes (e.g., scenes of vomiting/defecation) as working against the film's smarter elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raunchy elements are a double-edged criterion: they can be celebrated for boldness and equality in comedy, or criticised as excessive/alienating. Specific negative reactions are cited (e.g., 'we also need women that can crack you up without making you watch them have diarrhea').

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional honesty / thematic resonance
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics note the film is 'shrewdly honest about what's really going on in women's lives' and that emotional truth helps connect with audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond jokes, a film's ability to show authentic emotional stakes and relatable characters is treated as a key measure of its comedic and overall success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female-driven representation and cultural significance
rubrics_metrics.description: The film is described as a 'breakthrough for female-centered comedy' and a touchstone for discussion about women in comedy; it also passed the Bechdel test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation — having women in leading creative/performance roles and narratives centered on women — is evaluated both for cultural importance and as a factor in critical discourse about the film's impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical aggregator and polling metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Rotten Tomatoes: 89% (based on 292 reviews, avg 7.50/10); Metacritic: 75/100; CinemaScore: 'B+'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregate scores and audience polling are presented as quantitative indicators of critical and popular reception; these metrics are used to summarize consensus and compare films.

rubrics_metrics.name: Box office and commercial performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Grossed $306.5 million worldwide on a $32.5 million budget; opening weekend and domestic/international grosses cited; surpassed Knocked Up to become top-grossing Apatow Productions film.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial success (gross, opening weekend, return on budget, comparative performance) is used as an objective criterion for a film's market impact and as evidence of mainstream appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awards, nominations, and industry recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple nominations (Academy Awards, BAFTA, Golden Globes, WGA, SAG) and wins (critics' groups, MTV, etc.) are listed; WGA ranking and placement on later 'best of' lists noted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awards and inclusion on authoritative 'best of' lists function as retrospective validation and are used to assess artistic and industry esteem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone consistency and tonal control
rubrics_metrics.description: Some critics criticized the film's tonal inconsistency, saying crass or humiliating comedy undermines smarter deconstructions of female friendship and competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining a coherent tone (balancing crassness vs. smart social commentary) is highlighted as important; inconsistency is flagged as a weakness and given as a reason for detractors' negative reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting decisions and audition/improvisation practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Casting choices (e.g., selecting Rose Byrne as Helen because she wasn't a comedian) and audition practices (Rebel Wilson improvised for an hour) are described as influential. The writers' Groundlings background and table reads informed script development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Casting for the right tone/texture and encouraging improvisation in auditions/performances/table reads are presented as production techniques that shape comedic outcomes. Examples include improvised audition leading to casting and extended improvised scenes on Blu-ray.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production design and visual dichotomy (world-building)
rubrics_metrics.description: Production designer emphasized the film's two disparate worlds (Annie's Milwaukee vs. Helen's Chicago) and used locations and architecture to reinforce character and thematic contrasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual design and location choices are treated as criteria for supporting narrative and comedic contrasts between characters' lives; production design contributes to storytelling and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market and studio risk considerations for women-led comedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Director Paul Feig described Hollywood's attitude as an 'edict' testing whether a women-led comedy could succeed; producers 'sweated' because a failure might harm prospects for other films starring women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studio risk assessment and the perceived market viability for female-led comedies influence production decisions and are discussed as contextual criteria that affect whether projects get made and how they are positioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience composition and demographic reach
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal reported audience makeup: 33% male, 63% over age 30, indicating cross-demographic appeal contrary to expectations about bridesmaids concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demographic breakdowns (gender, age) are used to evaluate a film's reach and to challenge presumptions about who a film will attract; international success despite cultural specificity is noted as surprising evidence of broad appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural impact and legacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The film 'served as a touchstone for discussion about women in comedy' and has been ranked among best comedy films of the 21st century by several publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-term cultural influence, how a film shapes industry trends or discourse, and its placement on retrospective best-of lists are used as qualitative measures of significance beyond initial box office and reviews.
